studies.title: Four Months Of Open Road
studies.meaning: The surah opens by dissolving agreements rather than by attacking. A declaration of release is issued from God and His Messenger toward those treaty partners among the idolaters whose pacts are being ended, and then four months of free movement are granted. The grant is the point: the notice is public, the term is fixed, and the interval belongs to the other side. The closing clause tells them the delay should not be read as weakness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the ninth year after the migration, when Mecca had come under the community's authority and the annual pilgrimage was approaching. The commentators place the announcement in that pilgrimage season, read aloud to the assembled tribes. Surah 9 belongs to the last stretch of revelation, and its opening concerns arrangements with tribes whose agreements the classical sources describe as repeatedly broken.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be free or clear of something. It names the ending of an obligation rather than an act of war, which is why the sentence that follows sets a term instead of ordering an attack.
An imperative from a verb used of moving unhindered through open country. It offers the four months as safe passage across the land, not as a countdown watched from a distance.

A fixed span rather than an open one. The commentators differ over whether these are counted from the announcement or aligned with the calendar's sacred months, and they record both readings without settling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Treaties in that world were spoken, witnessed and held by memory, not filed. A pact could bind two tribes for a season or for years, and its terms were recited so that traders and travellers knew whose roads were safe. Ending one silently and then striking was the behaviour of a raider. Public renunciation before witnesses, with a stated interval, was how a party of standing withdrew.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 9 is the only surah in the Quran that does not open with the formula naming God as the Gracious and the Merciful. The classical commentators record more than one explanation, several linking the omission to the disavowal that begins it, and the early reciters preserved the surah in this form.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates a moral standard inside a political act. Even the ending of an agreement is given a form: it is announced rather than sprung, and it carries a term the other side is free to use. The final clause then removes the usual motive for such fairness, since the delay cannot be fear of being unable to prevail. What remains is that the manner of acting is itself required.

crossReferences.why: Sets the principle that a suspected pact is thrown back openly, on equal terms, before anything else is done.
Names the exception immediately: partners who kept their side are held to their full term.
Requires oaths to be fulfilled once made, and warns against unravelling what has been bound.

studies.applyIt: If you are ending something, a working arrangement or a standing favour, say so before you stop, and give the other person a date. Most of the damage in small withdrawals comes from the silence rather than from the decision. Notice costs you nothing except the discomfort of one conversation you would rather skip.

studies.title: A Proclamation At The Pilgrimage
studies.meaning: A second announcement follows, addressed not to treaty partners but to everyone gathered for the rites. God and His Messenger are quit of the idolaters. Then the sentence turns, and the turn carries the weight: if you repent, that is better for you. Only refusal draws the warning at the end. The proclamation is made in the one season when the whole peninsula could hear it at once.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year after the migration. The commentators place this at the pilgrimage of that year, when the announcement was recited to tribes assembled at Mecca. The choice of occasion is deliberate: the pilgrimage was the single gathering that drew people from across Arabia, so a proclamation made there reached everyone it concerned without a messenger being sent to each tribe separately.

keyTerms.note: From the root for hearing. The word names something proclaimed aloud so that nobody can later claim not to have been told, and the same root gives the call that summons people to prayer.
Commentators differ over what the greater refers to: the day of sacrifice, the standing at Arafat, or the full pilgrimage as distinct from the lesser visit made at other times of year.
The verb means literally to return. Repentance here is movement back toward something already known rather than the adoption of anything foreign, which is why it is offered to this audience at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The pilgrimage season was also the great fair. Tribes camped alongside each other, poets competed, debts were settled and caravan contracts made for the coming year. Truce customs held during the sacred months, so enemies stood in the same valley without fighting. Anything announced there travelled home in a hundred directions within weeks. It was the closest thing that world had to a public register.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause telling the addressees that they cannot escape God appears twice within three ayat, closing the grant of four months and then closing this proclamation. Repetition at that distance is uncommon outside the Quran's refrains, and it binds the interval that was given to the warning about what happens if it is spent doing nothing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The severity and the offer arrive in the same sentence, and the offer is placed first. That ordering says something about what the announcement is for. A break is declared, and in the next breath the way back is named as the better outcome for the people being broken with. Warning is reserved for the ones who turn away, which makes refusal, not identity, the thing being answered.

crossReferences.why: Spells out what repentance would mean in practice for the same people, and what follows from it.
Offers the same terms to opponents earlier: if they stop, what has passed is forgiven them.
States the general rule behind the offer, that no one should despair of God's mercy.

studies.applyIt: Notice which half of a hard message you deliver first. This proclamation states the break, then puts the way back before the consequence. When you next have to tell someone that something has ended, plan the order of your sentences before you speak, and put the door earlier than feels natural.

studies.title: Kept To The End Of Its Term
studies.meaning: An exception is carved out of the announcement just made, and its terms are exact. Treaty partners who kept every clause and backed nobody against the community are to have their agreement completed to its stated end. Nothing is renegotiated and no shorter term is substituted. The ayah then attaches what matters to character rather than to advantage, closing on the statement that God loves those who guard themselves.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, part of the same proclamation made at the pilgrimage. The commentators note that not every agreement with the surrounding tribes had failed, and that some were being honoured on both sides. This ayah addresses those cases. Read with the lines before and after it, it narrows the announcement of dissolution to partners whose own conduct had already ended the arrangement.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to diminish or reduce. It covers quiet erosion of an agreement rather than only open breach, so the test being applied is whether anything at all was taken away.
From a root for the back. To give someone your back is to stand behind them in a fight, so the word names material support given to an enemy rather than private sympathy.
From a verb meaning to guard or shield oneself. It describes someone who keeps a margin between themselves and wrongdoing, which is why it attaches here to a bargain nobody is enforcing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Agreements between tribes were remembered rather than written, so both sides watched for small subtractions: a delayed payment, a guide who failed to arrive, quiet help given to a rival at a watering place. A pact rarely collapsed in one act. It thinned. Everyone in that world could tell a partner who had drifted from one who had turned, and the difference decided who was safe on the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause that closes this ayah, that God loves those who guard themselves, is repeated word for word three ayat later at the end of 9:7. Both times it follows an instruction to keep faith with people whose agreements were still intact, so the surah uses one seal twice to mark the same limit.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A general announcement is immediately bounded by conduct. The passage does not treat a category of people as the unit of judgement; it treats what each party did with what it agreed. That puts responsibility on the record rather than on identity. By ending on divine love rather than on advantage, it also makes fidelity to an agreement a matter of what God values, not of what the stronger side can afford.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same limitation and closes with the identical clause about those who guard themselves.
Opens with the instruction to fulfil agreements, the general rule this exception is applying.
States that a pledge will be asked about, making an agreement something answered for later.

studies.applyIt: Think of an agreement you are keeping that nobody is checking: a rate you quoted, a deadline you set yourself, a promise made to someone who has forgotten it. Finish it on the original terms this week. This ayah treats an unenforced bargain as the place where character is actually visible.

studies.title: Bounded On Every Side
studies.meaning: This ayah is often quoted alone, and reading it in place changes what it says. It follows four months of notice and an exception for partners who kept their agreements, and it is followed at once by an order to protect any individual who asks for safety. Its own sentence suspends everything on their turning back, and then names God as forgiving and merciful. Every clause of it is conditional on something.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, within the proclamation made at the pilgrimage. The classical commentators read it against the open hostility described in the surrounding ayat, where parties are said to have broken oaths and started the fighting. They differ over its reach: some hold it addresses only those specific parties, while others read later ayat of the surah as qualifying it further. All read it alongside 9:4 and 9:6.

keyTerms.note: A vivid verb used of a skin coming off. It marks the months ending completely rather than fading out, which is what makes the term granted three ayat earlier a real and countable one.

Commentators differ over whether this names the four months of grace just granted or the four months of the traditional calendar in which fighting paused. Both readings are recorded without one being settled.
The verb means to leave something free and unobstructed. It releases entirely rather than granting a lesser standing, and the whole preceding sentence hangs on this clause.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia's roads belonged to whoever could hold them. A tribe at odds with another rarely met it in one battle; it watched the passes, waited at wells, and moved when the season allowed. The vocabulary of this ayah is the ordinary vocabulary of that conflict, the same words a poet would use of a raid. What has no equivalent in tribal practice is the clause that stops everything.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah ends on two of the commonest names of God in the Quran, the Forgiving and the Merciful, which are also the pair that opens almost every other surah and that this surah alone lacks at its head. The names absent from the opening of surah 9 appear instead at the close of its hardest line.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to make the conflict permanent. It is bounded by a term at one end and by a condition at the other, and the condition is one the other side can meet at any point, which places the ending in their hands rather than in the community's. It also fixes judgement on what people do next, the same standard the surah goes on to apply to believers themselves.

crossReferences.why: Immediately requires safe conduct for any individual seeking protection, and an escort home afterwards.
Exempts partners who kept their agreements, and stands as the limit read directly before this line.
States that those who did not fight you or drive you out are to be dealt with fairly.

studies.applyIt: When you next meet this ayah quoted on its own, read the four ayat around it before deciding what it says. The habit matters more than the single case: a sentence lifted out of its paragraph will usually claim something its neighbours refuse. Try it once this week on any passage someone hands you, from any book.

studies.title: Escort Him To Safety
studies.meaning: An individual from among the idolaters, party to no agreement, asks for protection. The instruction is to grant it, and then to grant two things more: he is to hear the speech of God, and afterwards to be escorted to wherever he is safe. Not converted, not held. The reason given is that these are people who do not know, which turns ignorance into a claim on protection rather than a charge against him.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, immediately after the hardest line of the proclamation. The commentators treat the placement as part of the sense: the same passage that ends the failed pacts opens a door for any individual belonging to those groups. They report that the granting of protection continued as an ordinary practice afterwards, and that a grant given by any member of the community was honoured by the rest.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb meaning to become a neighbour. In Arabian custom a person could claim shelter from a stranger simply by asking, and the request itself created an obligation the whole household carried.
A noun of place from the root for security. It names wherever this particular person is safe rather than a border or a camp, so the escort ends where his own safety begins.
The passage gives hearing as the purpose of the protection and then stops. Nothing follows about a response, and the journey home is promised whatever he decides to do with what he heard.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Granting protection was among the strongest obligations in Arabia. A man could arrive at a camp with enemies behind him, ask a stranger for shelter, and that stranger's tribe would then defend him at real cost. Refusing was a lasting disgrace, and poets kept the record of who had granted and who had refused. Everyone hearing this already knew the weight of the request being described.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah sits directly after the most severe line in the surah and reverses its direction inside a single sentence. The order is fixed in every arrangement of the text, and the classical commentators cite this ayah when discussing the reach of the one before it, which is why the two are rarely read apart in the exegetical tradition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates a conflict between parties from a duty owed to a person. Whatever the state of things between communities, an individual who asks is owed shelter, a hearing and a safe return. It also indicates how the Quran expects to persuade: the only thing the protected man is given is a chance to listen, and no particular outcome is demanded of him.

crossReferences.why: States that there is no compulsion in religion, the principle behind escorting him home either way.
Describes calling to God with wisdom and good argument rather than with pressure of any kind.
Shows how seriously grants of protection were taken as obligations within the early community.

studies.applyIt: Notice the two halves of the instruction: he is given a hearing, and he is given a way home. When you next explain something you believe to someone who disagrees, plan the second half as carefully as the first. Leave them a way to walk away that costs them nothing. Most people cannot hear anything while working out how to escape.

studies.title: As Long As They Hold Straight
studies.meaning: The question is put rhetorically and then answered against itself. How can there be a pact with parties who have shown what their pacts are worth, except with those who made theirs at the Sacred Mosque. For them the rule is reciprocal and phrased as a condition that keeps running: as long as they hold straight with you, hold straight with them. The measure is conduct, checked continuously rather than settled once.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, continuing the proclamation. The commentators identify the agreement made at the Sacred Mosque with the truce concluded some years earlier at Hudaybiyya and the arrangements that grew out of it. Several tribes were parties to those terms and had not broken them. The surah keeps naming this group separately, which is how it distinguishes an agreement that failed from a partner who failed.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to stand upright. The same word gives the straight path asked for in the opening surah, so the standard applied here to outside treaty partners is the one believers request for themselves.
Covers both a treaty between parties and a promise made before God. Arabic does not separate the political from the sworn in this word, which is why breaking one is treated as a religious matter.

The passage names the place where the agreement was made rather than the tribe that made it. The location carries the weight, since an undertaking given there was understood by all sides as given under sanctuary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sanctuary shaped how business was done. Around the House at Mecca, feuds paused, weapons were set aside, and men who would fight anywhere else stood together in one circle. Terms struck there carried more than their wording, because breaking them meant breaking the sanctuary as well. Tribes travelled to conclude agreements in that space precisely so the place would hold the other party to them.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for holding straight in this ayah comes from the same root as the request recited daily in the opening surah, guide us to the straight path. The Quran applies it to the conduct of treaty partners outside the community without changing the word, and closes the ayah with the same clause about divine love that closed 9:4.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets reciprocity as a floor rather than a ceiling. The community's conduct is tied to the other party's conduct, not to its beliefs, and the condition runs in the present, so it can be met again after being missed. That keeps the relationship open on terms anyone can read. It also implies that a pact's standing depends on being kept, which is a statement about obligation rather than about any group.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same exception for partners who kept their terms and ends with the same closing clause.
Recalls the pledge given during the truce negotiations whose terms this exception continues to protect.
Establishes the general obligation to fulfil agreements that this passage is applying narrowly.

studies.applyIt: Pick a relationship you have quietly downgraded because of something the other person did months ago. Ask yourself whether they are still doing it. The condition in this ayah runs in the present tense, which means it can stop applying. Most grudges survive because nobody ever re-checks the fact that started them.

studies.title: Pleasing You With Their Mouths
studies.meaning: The question from the previous ayah is picked up in one word and then answered by an observation about behaviour. Given the upper hand, these parties observe neither kinship nor obligation. What they offer instead is agreement in the mouth while the heart refuses, and the passage names the gap between the two without softening it. Pleasant words are not treated as evidence of anything.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, continuing the proclamation made at the pilgrimage. The commentators read the surrounding ayat as describing particular parties whose conduct after gaining an advantage had already been observed, rather than as a general characterisation of anyone. Surah 9 is unusually occupied with the distance between a stated position and actual conduct, and it turns the same scrutiny on people inside the community later.

keyTerms.note: A rare word the commentators explain variously as blood relation, a pact, or an oath sworn before God. The range itself is telling, since all three name a tie meant to hold without enforcement.
Names the responsibility a party takes on for someone under its guarantee. Disregarding it is not merely breaking a promise but abandoning a person who had been relying on that guarantee.
The Quran names the mouth rather than the tongue when it wants to isolate speech from whatever produced it. The contrast with the heart in the same clause is built into that choice of word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliances were spoken into being. Two men clasped hands, words were said before witnesses, and afterwards there was nothing else to point to. That made the social cost of a broken word enormous, and it made pleasant speech cheap for anyone willing to pay that cost. Traders learned to watch what a partner did when he held the advantage, because that was the only reliable test available.
studies.didYouKnow: The rare word for kinship in this ayah occurs only twice in the whole Quran, here and two ayat later at 9:10, both times in the same phrase paired with obligation. Its rarity is why the classical commentators record several explanations of it rather than one, and why English translations of the line visibly diverge.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes conduct under advantage the measure of a party's word. Anyone keeps an agreement while keeping it is convenient; the question posed is what happens when it stops being convenient. By setting mouth against heart in a single line, it also refuses to let sincerity be judged from the outside by pleasantness. That standard is applied to outsiders here and to insiders later in the surah.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same pair of words about kinship and obligation, extending the observation to how believers are treated.
Describes speech about worldly life that pleases the listener while the heart holds otherwise.
Portrays impressive speech from people whose loyalty lies elsewhere, using the same contrast.

studies.applyIt: Watch yourself for one week in the moments when you hold the advantage: a negotiation you are winning, a favour someone needs, an argument where you happen to be right. That is where this ayah puts the test. Note one occasion when you softened your words while conceding nothing, and say the harder true thing instead.

studies.title: Sold For A Small Price
studies.meaning: The charge is framed as a transaction. God's signs were exchanged for a small price, and the exchange had a consequence beyond the buyer: others were kept off the path. The image treats a decision about revelation as a purchase made badly, where what was received is not merely less than what was given but trivially so. The second ayah then applies the earlier observation to how a believer is treated.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, inside the pilgrimage proclamation. The commentators generally read the small price as immediate advantage: influence retained, wealth kept, standing among one's own people preserved. They report no single occasion for these two ayat, treating them instead as summarising conduct already described. The lines sit between an account of failed agreements and an offer of a different outcome three ayat later.

keyTerms.note: Ordinary commercial vocabulary. Applying it to revelation puts the choice in terms every listener recognised as a bad deal, where the buyer can see the price and takes it anyway.
Not a wrong price but a small one. The criticism is of proportion rather than of trading, and the Quran uses this exact pairing elsewhere of concealing what was known to be true.
The verb reaches past the subject to other people. What is being weighed is not only their own choice but its effect on everyone who was watching them make it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca lived on the pilgrimage. Custody of the House, the feeding and watering of pilgrims, and the trade arriving with them supported particular families whose standing depended on the arrangement continuing. Anyone in that position weighing a new claim about God was also weighing a livelihood. The commercial vocabulary here was not a metaphor reaching for an audience; it was that audience's own language for the actual decision.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for a small price recurs across the Quran, at 2:41, 2:79, 3:77, 5:44 and 16:95 among others, and in every one of its nine occurrences the thing exchanged is a covenant or a revealed sign rather than ordinary merchandise. The surah picks it up inside a passage otherwise concerned with treaties.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage frames rejection as a decision with a price attached rather than as an intellectual failure. That makes it answerable, since a person can be asked what they received. It also places the barring of others at the centre: what is condemned is not private disbelief but a position taken publicly enough to move other people. Using the language of trade assumes a listener able to judge value for themselves.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about exchanging God's signs for a small price, in an earlier community's setting.
Warns against selling a covenant with God cheaply, tying the image directly to broken oaths.
Supplies the observation about kinship and obligation that the second of these two ayat repeats.

studies.applyIt: Name the price. Whatever you are currently avoiding knowing, about your work, your health, or someone you are wronging, you are getting something for the avoidance. Write down in one line what it is. This passage's method is to ask what was received rather than to argue about the conclusion, and the answer is usually smaller than expected.

studies.title: Then They Are Your Brothers
studies.meaning: The sentence is short and its structure carries the argument. Three conditions, then a status: brothers in faith. Nothing is held back about what came before, no probationary category is created, and the word chosen is the strongest available for belonging. The closing clause says the signs are set out in detail for people who know, which attaches the whole passage to understanding rather than to enforcement.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, within the pilgrimage proclamation and directly after the ayat on tribes whose agreements had failed. The commentators notice the placement: the same section that ends the pacts specifies the terms on which former opponents become full members. The surah repeats this pattern, setting a hard passage beside an open door within a few lines of each other.

keyTerms.note: The word for full siblings, not for allies or associates. Arabic had gentler terms available for a newly formed relationship, and the passage declines to use any of them.
The same verb that gives the surah its name. It is used here of people who had been fighting the community, with no separate word marking their return as different from anyone else's.

keyTerms.gloss: and We set out in detail
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to separate into parts. It describes revelation articulated joint by joint rather than delivered whole, and the Quran pairs it here with knowing rather than with obeying.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Brotherhood was not a figure of speech. Blood ties decided who fed you in a famine, who paid compensation for your injuries, and who was obliged to fight alongside you. A man without kin had standing nowhere. In Medina the emigrants arrived with none of that and were paired with local households who took on exactly those obligations, so the community knew what the word cost when it was used.
studies.didYouKnow: The three conditions here, turning back, establishing the prayer and giving the due alms, appear in exactly the same order six ayat earlier at the close of 9:5, where they end that ayah rather than opening one. The repetition binds the two passages, so release there and belonging here rest on identical terms.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes membership turn on a present commitment rather than on a record. Someone who was an opponent yesterday is a brother today on the same terms as anyone else, with no residual category kept for the recently hostile. That is a claim about how God counts people, and it removes the instrument by which a victorious group would ordinarily keep former enemies permanently below itself.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the same three conditions, releasing rather than admitting, which binds the two ayat together.
States that believers are brothers, and draws the practical consequence of reconciling between them.
Recalls hearts joined after enmity, describing the transition this ayah sets terms for.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person you have forgiven in principle but still file under what they did. Do one ordinary thing with them this week that you would do with anyone else: share a meal, ask their advice, add them back to the group message. The passage does not ask for a feeling. It restores a status, and status shows in ordinary acts.

studies.title: So That They May Desist
studies.meaning: The condition has two parts and both are actions: breaking oaths after a pact, and attacking the religion. Only then does the instruction follow, and its object is specified as the leaders rather than a population. The parenthesis says they have no oaths left, meaning nothing remains that would hold them. The closing clause states the purpose, and the purpose is that they stop. Cessation, not conquest, is what the sentence aims at.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, inside the pilgrimage proclamation and immediately after the ayah on repentance and brotherhood. The commentators read the two together, the sequence marking the two directions open to the same parties. They connect the oath-breaking to specific incidents in the years following the truce, and the surah supplies its own account of who began the hostilities in the very next ayah.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of undoing spun thread back into loose fibre. It pictures a bond taken apart rather than snapped, and the Quran uses the same image elsewhere of a woman unpicking her own yarn.

The word names those who stand in front and are followed. Specifying leaders rather than a people narrows what follows to those directing the hostility, a point the commentators raise when discussing its scope.
From a root meaning to reach a limit. It names an end to the conduct rather than a defeat or a change of belief, and it is given as the purpose the whole instruction serves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribal fighting had a recognised shape: a raid, a counter-raid, intermediaries, compensation paid, and an agreed end. It stopped when both sides agreed it had stopped, and it was entirely possible for it never to stop. Feuds ran across generations because nobody could name a finishing point that both parties would accept. A stated purpose of desisting was, in that setting, a genuinely unfamiliar frame.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for breaking an oath here is the one the Quran uses at 16:92 of a woman who unravels her own spinning after making it strong. Both passages describe undoing something already completed, and the image explains why the surah treats oath-breaking as self-inflicted rather than as an injury done to the other party.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three limits are set in one sentence: a trigger in the other party's conduct, an object restricted to those leading it, and a purpose that expires when they stop. None of the three depends on what the other side believes; all three depend on what they do. Read whole, the ayah treats fighting as a response with a stated exit rather than as a settled condition.

crossReferences.why: States that fighting continues only until persecution ends, supplying the same kind of stopping point.
Uses the image of unravelling spun thread for breaking an oath after making it firm.
Supplies the record the instruction rests on: who broke oaths and who began the fighting.

studies.applyIt: Notice how the sentence ends. Before acting on a grievance, say out loud what would count as the matter being over. If you cannot finish that sentence, the grievance has no stopping point built into it and will not find one on its own. Write the ending first, even for something small this week.

studies.title: Is It Them You Fear
studies.meaning: A question is put to people who are hesitating, and it is built from facts rather than from exhortation. These are the ones who broke their oaths, who moved to expel the Messenger, and who started the hostilities. Then the question turns inward and asks whether it is them you fear. The answer offered is not that they are weak. It is that God has the better claim on that fear.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators tie the three charges to events the community had lived through: agreements undone, the plan against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the days before the migration, and hostilities begun by the other side. The surah is addressing believers who were genuinely reluctant, and it treats that reluctance as something to argue with rather than simply to condemn.

keyTerms.note: The particle at the front turns this into an urging rather than a request for information. Arabic uses the form when a speaker expects agreement and is asking why it has not yet arrived.
From the verb to start. The clause establishes who acted first, and the commentators treat it as part of the case being made rather than as incidental description.
A comparative built on the word for truth and right. It does not deny that fear of an enemy is real; it ranks two fears against each other and says which one has the stronger claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear was a practical calculation. A tribe counted the men it could field, the allies it could call on, and the distance to the nearest water, and then decided. Nobody thought less of a man for weighing those numbers carefully. What this ayah does is add a term to the calculation that cannot be counted, and it does so without telling the listeners their fear of an enemy was imaginary.
studies.didYouKnow: The three charges gathered into this one sentence are treated as separate matters elsewhere in the Quran. The plot to detain, kill or expel the Messenger before the migration is described at 8:30, in the surah placed immediately before this one, so a reader moving through the text in order has just encountered it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats hesitation as something to be reasoned with. It lays out evidence first and only afterwards reframes the emotion, and the reframing never claims the fear is unfounded. It introduces a larger object of fear and lets the smaller one stand in its shadow. That is a specific account of how conviction works: it displaces a fear rather than arguing it out of existence.

crossReferences.why: Describes the plot to detain, kill or expel the Prophet that this ayah refers back to.
Names fear of God as what replaces fear of an adversary, in almost the same structure.
Addresses another moment of hesitation later in this surah, using a very different argument.

studies.applyIt: Take the thing you are avoiding this week and write down what you are actually afraid of, in plain words, without softening it. Then write down what avoiding it costs you. The method here is to set two fears side by side rather than to talk one of them down. Do the comparison on paper, where you can see both.

studies.title: Heal The Chests Of Believers
studies.meaning: An instruction is given and then, unusually, its outcomes are listed, and most of them concern people's insides rather than the field. God will punish them at your hands, humiliate them, help you against them, heal the chests of a believing people, and take away the rage held in their hearts. Then the sequence stops and turns: God relents toward whom He wills. The list is closed before it becomes a verdict.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, continuing directly from the charges listed in the previous ayah. The commentators connect the healing spoken of here to members of the community who had suffered at the hands of the parties named, including those driven from their homes in Mecca and those who had lost relatives. The surah addresses people carrying grievances, and it names those grievances rather than passing over them.

keyTerms.note: The verb for curing an illness, used here of the chest rather than of the body. It treats a settled grievance as a condition needing treatment, which is a diagnosis rather than a reproach.
The Quran locates held feeling in the chest and understanding in the heart within it. Naming the chest points at what has been carried physically, the tightness of something held for years.
Not ordinary anger but the kind that is kept down and carried. Elsewhere the Quran praises those who restrain it; here it is something God removes rather than something the person manages.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Compensation for bloodshed existed because unresolved killing destroyed communities. A man with an unavenged brother carried it everywhere, and the obligation passed to his sons. Whole tribes arranged their alliances around wounds nobody alive had witnessed. The listeners knew exactly what a chest full of held rage did to a family across twenty years, and they knew settlements were negotiated precisely to stop it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the rage lifted here is the same one used at 3:134 of those who swallow their anger, where restraining it is listed among the qualities of people God loves. The Quran therefore uses one word both for something a person holds down and for something God takes away entirely.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The healing of grievance is counted among the purposes being served, which treats the inner state of a wronged community as mattering in itself rather than as a side effect. The passage then refuses to close the account. Having listed what will befall the other side, the final clause hands their future back to God's decision, which stops the reader from taking the list as a settled judgement on particular people.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for rage, there among the qualities of those who restrain it.
Sets pardon beside the right to respond, and prefers the one who forgives and reconciles.
Holds out affection between present enemies as possible, which the closing clause here leaves open.

studies.applyIt: Find the grievance you have stopped mentioning because you assume nothing can be done about it. Say it once, to one person, in a single sentence. This passage treats a chest that has carried something for years as an actual injury rather than a weakness of character, and the first thing done for an injury is that somebody names it.

studies.title: No Confidant Slipped In
studies.meaning: The question is put to people who have just been told to fight, and it does not defend the instruction. It asks what they had expected. Being left alone is named as the assumption being corrected, and what corrects it is knowledge becoming visible: God distinguishing those who strive and who have taken no confidant outside the community. The word for that confidant is not the ordinary word for a friend. It names someone slipped in.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, following the ayat on parties who broke their agreements. The commentators read the question as addressed to the community itself rather than to any opponent, and they connect it to the surah's larger concern with commitments that had not yet been tested by anything costly. Comparable questions appear at moments in Medina when a demand separated stated allegiance from acted allegiance.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to enter or be inserted. It names someone taken into confidence from outside, and the image is of a thing pushed in where it does not belong rather than an alliance declared openly.
The passive of a verb meaning to abandon or leave be. The question assumes that being left untested is what the listeners had quietly expected, and it treats that expectation itself as the error.
The commentators explain that divine knowledge is not acquired, so this phrase names knowledge becoming visible in what people actually do rather than something God comes to find out.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Loyalty in that society ran through named relationships everyone could see: kin, allies, clients. A quiet understanding with a rival party was possible but dangerous, because it was the kind of thing that eventually surfaced and destroyed a man's standing for good. The word used here belongs to that world of private arrangements, the second commitment kept in reserve in case the first went badly.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for a confidant taken in from outside occurs only once in the entire Quran, here in this ayah. Its rarity left the classical commentators with no parallel passage to compare it against, so they explained it from the verb's ordinary sense of entering or being inserted, which is why English versions render it so variously.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats testing as the means by which a claim becomes a fact rather than as a punishment. Nothing is added to what God knows; what changes is what exists to be known. That locates the value of a hard moment in what it produces rather than in what it proves. And by naming a hidden second loyalty as the thing being sorted out, it puts sincerity in what a person holds back.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question directly: do people think they will be left saying we believe without being tested.
Denies entry to the garden before God has distinguished those who struggled among you.
Recalls earlier communities shaken until even the messenger asked when God's help would come.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you are keeping in reserve. Most people run a quiet second plan alongside the thing they say they are committed to, and the plan is usually sensible. Name yours this week in one sentence, without deciding to abandon it. Seeing it clearly is the whole exercise, and it changes how the first commitment feels.

studies.title: Witnesses Against Themselves
studies.meaning: A disqualification is stated, and the reason given is self-contradiction rather than hostility. Those who bear witness against themselves by their own profession are not the ones to keep God's places of worship. The sentence turns on that testimony: nobody needs to investigate them, because they have said it. Their works are then described as coming to nothing, which is a statement about what those works were resting on all along.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators connect these ayat to the custodianship of the sanctuary at Mecca, an office certain families had held for generations and which carried both prestige and income. The claim to that role was being settled after the city changed hands. The passage answers a question about entitlement to a religious position rather than about who may enter a building.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers building, maintaining, and filling a place with life. Arabic uses the same root for a house that is inhabited, so the word names custody in active use rather than ownership.
A legal image. Testimony against oneself needs no corroboration, so the passage treats an open profession as settling the matter without any accusation having to be brought by anyone.
Used of an animal that swells from bad pasture and then dies. The image is of something that looked like growth and was not, and it is applied here to a lifetime of accumulated works.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The offices of the sanctuary were real property. Feeding pilgrims, supplying water, holding the keys and hosting delegations were divided among particular clans, passed from father to son, and argued over in poetry. They brought standing across the whole peninsula and a season's income. Losing a claim to one changed a family's position in a way everyone in Mecca would notice within days.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for tending God's places of worship appears twice in successive ayat here, once denied and once affirmed, so the two lines answer each other word for word. The same root gives the Arabic words for a lifetime and for an inhabited settlement, so the term carries the sense of a building kept alive by being used.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the running of a sacred place from a claim upon it. A religious office is treated as resting on something the officeholder affirms, so it cannot be inherited past the point where the affirmation stops. That is a claim about what makes custodianship legitimate at all. It also accepts a person's own stated position as sufficient testimony, which removes any need to inspect what is inside anyone.

crossReferences.why: States the positive form of the same rule in the next ayah, listing who does tend them.
Describes the House appointed for those who circle it, stand there and bow in prayer.
Discusses those who prevent God's name from being mentioned in places of worship.

studies.applyIt: Think of a role you hold that came to you by history rather than by choice: a family duty, a committee seat, a title at work. Ask whether you still affirm the thing it exists for. If you do, say so out loud once this week. If you do not, this passage would have you notice the gap rather than look away from it.

studies.title: Fears None But God
studies.meaning: The positive form arrives as a list, and the list is deliberately ordinary: belief in God and the last day, keeping up the prayer, giving what is due, and fearing no one but God. Lineage and office do not appear. Then the closing clause pulls back from certainty and says such people may well be among the guided, using a particle of hope rather than a guarantee, so the verdict stays where it belongs.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, answering the previous ayah directly. The commentators read the two as a single argument about who has a claim on the sanctuary once Mecca had come under the community's authority. In that setting the list given here was pointedly unremarkable: it names things anyone at all could do, in place of the hereditary services that had decided the question for generations.

keyTerms.note: A restrictive particle. It does not soften the previous ayah but narrows the field to a single group, which is why the two lines are read together as a denial followed by a definition.
This verb names fear mixed with awe rather than fright. Placing it last makes it the item holding the others upright, since each of the earlier ones can be performed for an audience.

A particle of hope. After listing the strongest qualifications available the sentence still declines to certify anyone, which the commentators note as characteristic of how the Quran speaks of final standing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Status in Mecca was inherited and visible. A man's clan decided where he sat, whom he could marry, and whether his word carried weight in a dispute. Against that, the qualifications listed here could be satisfied by a newcomer with no ancestry within a month of arriving. To the families who had held the sanctuary's offices, the list would have sounded like a description of nobody in particular.
studies.didYouKnow: The particle of hope that closes this ayah is the one the Quran uses when it withholds certainty, and here it follows the strongest set of credentials the passage can assemble. Even someone meeting every item is called only likely to be among the guided, which is how the surah keeps the final verdict out of human hands.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage replaces inherited standing with present practice and then refuses to turn practice into a guarantee. Both moves matter. The first opens a sacred role to anyone at all; the second stops that opening from hardening into a new hierarchy of the certified. What remains is a description of a life, deliberately held apart from any claim about where that life finally arrives.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule negatively in the previous ayah, which this one answers point by point.
Describes men whose trade and selling never distract them from the remembrance of God.
States that places of worship belong to God, so no one else is called upon inside them.

studies.applyIt: Look at the last item on the list: fearing no one but God. Pick one thing you did this week partly because of who was watching, and do the same thing tomorrow with nobody watching at all. Not a larger version. The identical act, unobserved, so you can feel for yourself whether the motive changes.

studies.title: Water For The Pilgrims
studies.meaning: Two things are set beside each other and the comparison is then refused. Giving water to pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque, both genuine services, are placed next to belief and striving, and the verdict is that they do not weigh the same with God. What is being measured is not the usefulness of the service but the standing of the one performing it. The error is named as wrongdoing, not as miscalculation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators report a dispute over whether the hereditary services of the sanctuary ranked alongside faith and struggle, and they place this ayah as the answer to it. Those services were prestigious offices held by particular families, and the question came from people whose position rested on them. The surrounding ayat approach the same subject from several directions in turn.

keyTerms.note: A named office rather than an act of kindness. It covered the wells, the transport and the sweetened drink distributed during the season, and one family in particular carried the responsibility.
A verb of levelling, used of two things placed on the same scale. The Quran repeats this construction to refuse comparisons that its audience had already assumed were reasonable ones.
From a root meaning to put a thing where it does not belong. Applied to a misjudgement about rank, it says the fault is one of arrangement rather than of missing information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: During the pilgrimage season water was the difficulty everything turned on. Mecca sat in a dry valley and tens of thousands of visitors arrived within a few days. Drawing, carrying and distributing water for them was a serious operation needing men, animals and money, and the family who managed it was honoured for it across Arabia. The service being weighed here was real and expensive.
studies.didYouKnow: The construction used to refuse a comparison, saying that two things are not equal, recurs across the Quran to reject pairings its listeners found natural: the blind and the seeing, the living and the dead, those who know and those who do not. This ayah applies the identical formula to a religious office and a personal commitment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not deny that the service is good. It denies that performing it settles anything about the performer. That distinction stops public religious work from functioning as a credential, and it makes the interior question unavoidable for people whose outward record is excellent. It also removes an argument that any established religious institution can make about itself on the strength of what it maintains.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same formula of inequality, beginning with the blind and the one who sees.
Approaches the same claim on the sanctuary's offices from the side of who may keep them.
States that neither flesh nor blood of offerings reaches God, but the awareness behind them.

studies.applyIt: Name the piece of visible good work you would mention first if someone questioned your character. Then, for one week, do not mention it to anyone. Notice how much of your sense of standing was resting on being able to point at it. The passage is not against the work. It is against the resting.

studies.title: Greater In Degree With God
studies.meaning: Three things are named in sequence, believing, leaving home, and striving with property and person, and what follows is a rank rather than a reward. The wording is comparative: greater in degree with God. A second sentence then names them with a word drawn from contests, the ones who have won. The outcome is spoken of as already settled, which is unusual for a description of living people.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, continuing the answer to the dispute about rank in the previous ayah. The commentators read the three terms as describing the emigrants in particular, people who had left property and family behind in Mecca. The ayah is not making an abstract statement; it names the group whose standing had just been compared unfavourably by those holding the sanctuary's hereditary offices.

keyTerms.note: From the word for a stair. The Quran uses it of ranks differing by increments rather than in kind, so the comparison here runs on one scale with the services mentioned just before.
This pairing occurs seven times in the Quran and keeps the same order every time, property before person. The order matters, since property is what most people are asked for and rarely offer first.
From a verb meaning to succeed or to draw the winning lot. It belongs to the vocabulary of contests, and the Quran reserves it for outcomes treated as settled rather than hoped for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Emigration meant leaving a house that could not be sold, debts that could not be collected, and a clan that would no longer answer for you. Some who left Mecca arrived with nothing and were still poor years afterwards. Their neighbours in Medina had watched them arrive. When this ayah speaks of wealth and person together, the audience could put names to both halves of the phrase.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase pairing wealth and person occurs seven times in the Quran and keeps the same order in every one of them, property named before the self. Four of those seven are in this surah alone, which is more than in any other, and the commentators read the fixed order as tracking the actual sequence in which a commitment costs something.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a question about rank by giving one, which the Quran usually declines to do. Elsewhere such comparisons are withheld; here an explicit one is made and then sealed with a settled verdict. The confidence attaches to a description rather than to named individuals, so nobody is certified personally, and the door stays open to anyone prepared to meet the description.

crossReferences.why: Distinguishes those who strive with wealth and person from those who sit, by a degree.
Poses the comparison this ayah answers, weighing the sanctuary's offices against faith and struggle.
Names the same commitment of wealth and person and calls it a trade that saves.

studies.applyIt: Notice the order inside the phrase: wealth first, then self. Most people reverse it, offering time and effort freely while keeping money out of the conversation. This week, give away an amount you actually feel, before you volunteer for anything at all. The order is the point of the exercise.

studies.title: Mercy, Acceptance, And Gardens
studies.meaning: Good news is announced in three parts, and the order of the three is the point. Mercy from Him, then acceptance, then gardens holding a bliss described as settled rather than passing. A single word afterwards extends it without end, and the closing line names the reward as great. The sequence moves from something given, to God being pleased with them, to a place, and the place comes last.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, directly following the naming of those who believed, emigrated and struggled. The commentators note that the good news is announced to people whose standing had just been questioned in a dispute over religious office. The answer offered is not an argument but a promise. The surah pairs struggle with the garden again at 9:72 and at 9:111.

keyTerms.note: From a root connected with the skin, since news shows first in the face. The verb names the delivery of good news specifically, and Arabic keeps a separate word for the delivery of bad.
An intensive form of a word for being satisfied with something. The commentators treat it as the greatest item in this list, since the gardens are a place while this names a relation.
The second word means residing or staying put. It rules out the quality every earthly pleasure has of already being on its way elsewhere, which is what the promise is set against.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bliss that stays was not an obvious idea there. In that climate everything good was seasonal: pasture after rain, dates for a few weeks, a well that held until it did not. Wealth travelled with caravans and could vanish in a single afternoon. A watered garden was the standard image of security precisely because it was the rarest one, and everyone knew how quickly one could fail.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for God's acceptance is placed here between mercy and the gardens, and later in this same surah, at 9:72, the text states outright that acceptance from God is greater than the gardens themselves. The commentators read the two passages together, since the ordering of this list already implies what the later ayah says plainly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places a relation with God above a place given by God, and it does so by arranging a list rather than by arguing. That arrangement says the destination is not the point of the destination. It also delivers the outcome as news already true rather than as an incentive being dangled, which changes what the promise is doing: it reports rather than bargains.

crossReferences.why: States in this same surah that acceptance from God is greater than the gardens themselves.
Joins the same two elements, God pleased with them and they with Him, at a surah's close.
Lists gardens, pure companions and acceptance from God, ending on the same term.

studies.applyIt: Read the three items in order and notice which one you would have put first. Most people reach for the place. Sit with the middle one tonight for a minute: not what you are given, but being found acceptable. It is a different kind of hope, and harder to picture, which is part of why the list runs this way.

studies.title: When Two Loyalties Pull Apart
studies.meaning: The instruction is narrow and carries its condition inside it. Fathers and brothers are not to be taken as allies if they have chosen disbelief over belief. The word used is the one for protective alliance in a conflict, not the one for kindness or company. What is being addressed is where a person stands when two loyalties actually pull apart, which in that year they did, and the ayah does not pretend otherwise.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, when households were split by an active conflict and some members were carrying information between the two sides. The commentators read the ayah against that situation rather than as a general rule about relatives, and they set it alongside the passages requiring good treatment of parents who do not share a person's faith. The surah returns to divided families more than once.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning nearness. In this period the word named the party you fought alongside and who answered for you, so it carries obligations of defence rather than warmth of feeling.
A form of the verb to love meaning to prefer one thing deliberately over another. It names a settled choice rather than a condition someone was simply born into and never examined.
From putting a thing where it does not belong. The charge concerns misplaced loyalty rather than belief, which fits a passage about which side a person stands on during a conflict.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Kinship was the security system. Your father's line fed you, paid your debts, avenged you, and was answerable for what you did. Choosing a loyalty that cut across it left a person genuinely exposed. In the years after the migration there were households divided between two cities at war, and some men had fathers on the other side of a battle line, which both sides knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses different vocabulary for family duty and for political alliance, and this ayah uses only the second. The passages requiring kind treatment of parents who press a person to abandon their faith, at 31:15 and 29:8, use the first, and classical commentaries on this ayah routinely cite them alongside it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage distinguishes between honouring people and being on their side in a fight. It concedes that the two can come apart, which most moral traditions prefer not to state, and it says what to do when they do. It also refuses to let the strength of a family tie decide a question of allegiance by itself, while leaving the tie and its duties standing.

crossReferences.why: Requires kind company with parents even while refusing them on the one point at issue.
Makes the same distinction, joining a refusal on one matter with good treatment overall.
Describes the same division running through families, in the strongest terms the Quran uses.

studies.applyIt: Separate the two questions this ayah separates. Think of a relative you disagree with deeply, and write down one thing you owe them that has nothing to do with the disagreement: a phone call, a debt, a visit. Do that one thing this week. Duty is the half most people drop first, and it is the half the Quran keeps.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: Eight Things You Love
studies.meaning: Eight things are listed, and the list is generous rather than dismissive: parents, children, siblings, spouses, kin, wealth you earned, a trade whose slump you fear, homes you are content in. Each is something a decent person would love. Nothing in the list is condemned. The sentence asks only what happens when they are set against God, the Messenger and struggle in His way, and then it stops and says wait.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators place this in the period when leaving Mecca, and later joining the difficult march north, cost people exactly the things named. Trade routes, houses and family ties were the actual price being paid. The surah addresses an audience being asked to choose rather than one weighing the question in the abstract, which is why the list is so specific.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to gain by one's own effort and carries a note of labour. The wealth in this list is not inherited, which makes the attachment to it more understandable rather than less so.
A commercial term for stagnant goods that nobody is buying. The fear named is not poverty but a market going quiet, which was the specific anxiety of a merchant town.

keyTerms.gloss: then wait, then watch for it
keyTerms.note: An imperative meaning to await an outcome. The sentence breaks off rather than issuing a threat, leaving the listener holding a decision that has not been made for them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a trading city whose families lived on two great caravans a year. A season of slow business could ruin a household, and a merchant's standing rose and fell with his ability to move goods. The eight items here are the exact contents of a comfortable life in that town, named roughly in the order a man would have lost them by making a costly commitment.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the longest list of competing attachments anywhere in the Quran, and it moves outward from the household to the market and back to the house again. Nothing in it is criticised. The whole force of the ayah rests on one comparative word, dearer, which sets the eight against three without ever calling the eight worthless.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assumes that love is ranked rather than exclusive. It does not ask anyone to stop loving eight ordinary things; it asks what happens at the point of conflict, which is the only place a ranking ever becomes visible. And by ending in an instruction to wait rather than in a verdict, it leaves the ranking to be revealed by events instead of settled by a declaration.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who love God more intensely than anything else, using the same comparative form.
Makes love of God testable by following the Messenger, giving an abstract claim a measure.
Warns against wealth and children drawing a person away from the remembrance of God.

studies.applyIt: Write the list out for yourself: the eight things in your own life that correspond to the ones named here. Do not rank them against anything. Just write them, and notice which one you hesitated over, or quietly left off. That hesitation is the ayah's real question, and it usually arrives before any conclusion does.

studies.title: The Day Your Numbers Pleased You
studies.meaning: A record of help is recalled and then a reversal inside it. God gave you victory in many places, the sentence begins, and then names one day where that was not what happened first. Your own numbers pleased you, and they availed you nothing. The earth, wide as it was, closed in, and you turned your backs. The pleasure taken in a count is named as the thing that went wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators identify the day named here as an engagement in a valley shortly after Mecca came under the community's authority, when the assembled force was the largest yet gathered and is reported in the sources at around twelve thousand. Archers placed above the valley broke the leading ranks at the outset, and the line gave way before it could be reformed. The surah recalls it to people who were there.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning wonder. The form makes the numbers the subject and the listeners the object, so the passage describes something that happened to them rather than a decision they took.
An abstract noun meaning abundance. Naming the count itself rather than the army makes the sentence about a quantity, which is precisely the thing the passage says was being relied on.
The verb for a space becoming too small. Applied to open ground, and described in the same breath as spacious, it names a fear that changes what a place is rather than what it measures.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Numbers usually did decide these things. A force visibly larger often ended a confrontation before it began, and tribes calculated carefully before committing anyone. Ground mattered just as much: a valley with high sides was where a smaller force could undo a bigger one, and every man in that army knew it. The reversal described here was militarily ordinary and personally humiliating.
studies.didYouKnow: Only two engagements are named by place anywhere in the Quran: one at 3:123 and this valley here. The surah recalls its day not as a victory but as the moment the community's confidence in its own size failed, which is an unusual way for any account to speak about its own side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attributes a failure to a feeling rather than to an error of planning. What went wrong was pleasure taken in a number, and the help that had come in many places did not arrive while that pleasure held. It also tells the story with the community itself as the subject of the failure, which limits how any later generation can read its own successes back into the text.

crossReferences.why: Recalls an earlier day when the same community was few in number and was helped regardless.
Reminds them of a time when they were few and feared being seized by people.
Continues the account, describing the calm sent down and the rally that followed the break.

studies.applyIt: Find the number you are quietly relying on: savings, followers, years of experience, people who would take your call. Say in one sentence what it actually protects you from, and then say what it does not. The ayah does not tell you the number is nothing. It tells you what happens when the number is what pleases you.

studies.title: Then He Sent Down Calm
studies.meaning: The recovery is described in three moves and not one of them belongs to the men on the ground. Calm was sent down on the Messenger and on the believers, forces nobody could see were sent down, and the other side met what it met. Then the account stops entirely and says God will relent afterwards toward whom He wills. A battle narrative closes on the possibility of forgiveness for the defeated.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing directly from the reversal in the valley recalled in the previous ayah. The commentators describe the line reforming around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) after the initial break, and the day ending very differently from how it began. The classical sources also report that many of those defeated came to terms with the community afterwards, which the commentaries connect to the closing line here.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be still or to dwell. The word names steadiness settling on people rather than courage summoned by them, and the Quran uses it at other moments of extreme pressure.

The phrase declines to describe what was sent. Commentators note that the Quran repeatedly mentions unseen help in exactly this form, which keeps the account from becoming a description of the invisible.
The verb for repentance with God as its subject and a person as its object. Arabic makes the turning mutual, so one word covers a person returning and God turning toward them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A broken line rarely reformed. Once men began running in a valley the day was usually finished, and the survivors were counted afterwards. Any account of a rally after a rout would have struck an audience who knew how these things went as genuinely remarkable. What follows, that the defeated might later be turned toward, was equally unusual in a world where a beaten tribe expected terms rather than welcome.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the calm sent down here occurs six times in the Quran: twice in this surah, at this ayah and again at 9:40 for the night in the cave, three times in surah 48, and once in surah 2. Wherever it comes upon people it is sent rather than summoned, which is why the commentaries treat it as a gift.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage removes the community's agency from its own recovery, and then removes its authority over the outcome for the other side. Calm was sent, help was sent, and the final word about the defeated belongs to God alone. Taken together the two ayat make a victory into something received rather than achieved, which is a difficult thing to say immediately after winning one.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for calm sent down, there in a cave rather than on a field.
Describes the same calm descending into the hearts of believers so that their faith increases.
Describes a drowsiness sent as security after a hard day, in closely similar language.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time something you were sure would break did not, and you have quietly taken credit for it since. Write one sentence naming what you actually contributed, and one naming what you did not arrange. This passage tells a rally without giving anyone on the field the credit, which is worth doing once with a story of your own.

studies.title: If You Fear Poverty
studies.meaning: Two things are said and the second takes up more room than the first. Those who associate others with God are described with a word for impurity, and are not to approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs. Then the passage turns to what its audience was actually worried about, which was money. If you fear want, God will enrich you from His bounty if He wills. The anxiety is named rather than dismissed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, the year of the proclamation at the pilgrimage. The commentators explain the fear of want from the economics of Mecca, a town that lived on the trade the pilgrimage brought in. Removing a large body of visitors threatened the city's income directly. The classical commentaries discuss the word rendered as impure at length, most reading it of the condition of idolatry rather than of anything bodily.

keyTerms.note: The commentators differ over its sense. Most read it of the condition of associating others with God rather than of the body, and they note that the word stands here as a noun rather than the usual adjective.
A word for the poverty of a household with dependants rather than personal hardship. It names the fear of being unable to provide, which is why the answer given speaks of enrichment.
The word means overflow or surplus, what is there beyond need. The reassurance names a source rather than an amount, and it is immediately qualified with if He wills.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The pilgrimage season was Mecca's harvest. Grain, cloth, leather and livestock changed hands within a few weeks, and families lived off it for the rest of the year. A fall in visitor numbers was not an abstraction; it was the difference between a household eating well and a household borrowing. The fear this ayah names would have been the first subject discussed in the markets that season.
studies.didYouKnow: The reassurance about poverty takes up more words in this ayah than the instruction that prompted it, and it closes on a conditional, if He wills, rather than a flat promise. The Quran attaches that same qualification to several of its assurances about provision, which the commentators read as keeping a promise from being taken for a mechanism.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes an economic fear seriously enough to answer it in the same breath as the instruction that caused it. That says something about how people are addressed here: an objection is anticipated rather than left to be raised later. And the answer offered is not a calculation about replacement trade. It relocates the source of livelihood entirely, which is a claim about where provision comes from at all.

crossReferences.why: Promises provision from a direction not reckoned on, to whoever is conscious of God.
States that the provision of every creature that moves on earth rests with God.
Places provision in the heaven, along with everything people are being promised.

studies.applyIt: Name the specific financial fear sitting underneath a decision you keep postponing. Not the decision, the fear, and the number if there is one. This ayah answers an anxiety it first allows to be spoken aloud. Most people skip that step, which is why reassurance so often fails to land anywhere in particular.

studies.title: A Frontier And A Payment
studies.meaning: The instruction is directed at a described group, and the description has four parts: not believing in God or the last day, not treating as forbidden what God and His Messenger have, and not following the religion of truth, from among those who were given the Book. It then names a stopping point, which is a payment rather than a removal. Commentators differ over who is included and over what the closing phrase describes.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year. The commentators place this passage in the run-up to the expedition north toward Tabuk, on the frontier with Byzantine territory, where the community expected to meet an organised state rather than tribes. Almost everything that follows in the surah concerns that march. The classical sources describe the payment named here as standing in place of military service, with those unable to fight exempt from it.

keyTerms.note: Commentators connect the word to a root meaning to suffice or to requite. They describe it as levied on able adult men in place of military service, with the young, the old and the poor exempt from it.

A phrase whose sense is genuinely disputed. Recorded readings include paid directly rather than through an agent, paid out of one's own capacity, and paid in acknowledgement of the arrangement itself.
The word for religion here covers practice and obligation as much as belief, and the same root gives the Arabic word for a debt, meaning something owed and later answered for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The northern frontier was a different world from tribal Arabia. Byzantine garrisons, salaried troops and taxed provinces lay beyond the desert, and Arab tribes along the border had long paid tribute to one empire or another. Payment in exchange for protection and exemption from service was the ordinary arrangement everyone in that region already understood, on both sides of the line.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only ayah in the Quran that mentions the payment named here, and the two-word phrase describing how it is handed over occurs nowhere else either. That is why the classical commentaries devote unusual space to these few words and record several readings of them rather than settling on a single one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a terminus. What it describes begins in conduct on a frontier and ends in an arrangement rather than in a conversion or a removal, and the classical tradition describes that arrangement as carrying protection in return. The commentators' unresolved differences over its scope are themselves part of what has been transmitted: the passage was never received as self-evident.

crossReferences.why: Ends on a comparable stopping point, so that neither passage describes an open-ended condition.
States that fairness toward those who did not fight you or expel you is not prohibited.
States there is no compulsion in religion, which commentators cite when discussing this passage's reach.

studies.applyIt: When a passage is contested among the people who studied it longest, the honest response is to say so. Practise that this week on something you half know: answer a question with the range of views rather than the one you happen to prefer, and notice how much harder that is than sounding certain.

studies.title: Said Out Of Their Mouths
studies.meaning: Two statements are quoted and both are answered the same way: these are their sayings, out of their mouths. That phrase carries the argument. It puts the claim at the level of speech without conceding it any grounding, and then sets it in line with what earlier rejecters had said. Neither statement is argued against here. The passage answers with a refusal and then asks how a view like that takes hold at all.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, ninth year, in the section preparing for the march north where communities of the Book would be met. The commentators note that the first statement quoted is attributed to a particular group of people who said it rather than to everyone, and they discuss who held it and how widely.
